vignette: Ali, a 40-year-old Middle Eastern man and software engineer, has been struggling with the aftermath of a devastating natural disaster that struck his hometown two years ago. The event was traumatic not just for its intensity but also because Ali had been caught in the midst of it, experiencing firsthand the chaos and loss. Since then, he has found himself reacting to everyday stimuli as if they were threats-a constant state of heightened alertness that leaves him feeling perpetually on edge. Ali's wife has noticed his increasing anxiety over minor events; a sudden noise or an unexpected touch can trigger a severe startle response. He always checks for escape routes before settling into any space, and even simple tasks at work now feel laden with potential danger. This heightened vigilance is not just a reaction to the environment but also a consequence of Ali's deeply held belief that he cannot trust his surroundings or himself. What frightens him most is the sense that nothing good can happen to him anymore-a stark contrast to the happy and carefree person he used to be. He often thinks, "Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation," which only exacerbates his feelings of vulnerability. This belief feeds a constant cycle where he feels as though he is always in danger. Ali's memories of the disaster are vivid and fragmented; he cannot put them in order, but when they do come back, it feels like reliving the event all over again. The auditory recall is particularly troubling: he hears sounds from that day as if they were happening right now. These intrusive memories often lead him to ruminate about getting revenge on those who caused his distress, though he knows such thoughts are unproductive and unhealthy. The intensity of these memories has led Ali to engage in maladaptive coping strategies, one being the forced positive reframing of situations. He tries to think only positive thoughts as a way to distract himself from the overwhelming fear and confusion. However, this approach often backfires; it creates a sense that he is not truly confronting his feelings or addressing the underlying issues. The more Ali ruminates on revenge and isolates himself from medical cues like hospitals and physical examinations, the deeper he sinks into negative appraisals of self-worth and future prospects. This negative cycle reinforces itself, as these thoughts make him even more vigilant about threats and cause his memories to be more intrusive. His work as a software engineer has been affected significantly. He avoids situations where there might be unexpected movements or touches from colleagues, which isolates him socially at the office. The fear that he cannot trust his environment or himself to handle such stimuli leads him to avoid social gatherings altogether. This avoidance and hyper-vigilance have strained his relationships with coworkers, leaving him feeling isolated. Ali's current state is a complex interplay of these factors. He had come to believe that forcing positive thoughts would protect him from the memories, but it has only made things worse. His relationship with his wife is also under strain as he withdraws emotionally and physically from her touch. What finally brought Ali to seek help was an incident at work where a sudden movement in the office caused him to have a panic attack. He realized that these reactions were taking over his life and affecting those around him. Despite feeling that nothing good can happen, he hopes for relief from the constant state of fear and distress. His primary goal is finding a way to regain control and return to the happy person he once was. Ali's journey towards recovery will require addressing not just the symptoms but also the underlying beliefs that perpetuate his distress. The cycle of negative appraisals, threat perception, intrusive memories, and maladaptive coping strategies must be broken for him to move forward.
